# Summary

Intravenous (IV) iron therapy in heart failure with iron deficiency (ID) improves exercise capacity and reduces heart failure hospitalizations, whereas oral (PO) iron shows inconsistent benefits on functional measures and limited effects on key laboratory endpoints. Across randomized trials and network meta-analyses, IV iron significantly increases 6-min walk distance (6MWD), improves NYHA class and quality of life, raises ferritin, increases transferrin saturation, and lowers HF hospitalization risk, with no excess mortality or serious adverse events. In contrast, PO iron yields uncertain gains in 6MWD and less reliable improvements in ferritin and TSAT, and is often limited by gastrointestinal intolerance. Overall, IV iron is the preferred strategy to improve symptoms and reduce hospitalizations, while PO iron may be considered when IV therapy is inaccessible.

# Evidence on Exercise Capacity

- IV iron significantly improves functional capacity. In a large randomized trial (CONFIRM-HF), IV ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) increased 6MWD by 33 m at 24 weeks versus placebo, with effects sustained at 52 weeks (+36 m). Improvements in NYHA class, patient global assessment, quality of life, and fatigue were observed from 24 weeks onward. IV FCM also reduced hospitalizations for worsening HF (hazard ratio 0.39, 95% CI 0.19–0.82) without increasing mortality or serious adverse events. <cite id="25176939">Treatment with FCM significantly prolonged 6MWD at Week 24 (difference FCM vs. placebo: 33 ± 11 m, P = 0.002), with effects sustained to Week 52 (36 ± 11 m, P < 0.001), and was associated with a significant reduction in hospitalizations for worsening HF (0.39, 95% CI 0.19–0.82, P = 0.009), while deaths and adverse events were comparable.</cite>

- Network meta-analysis corroborates IV iron's functional benefits. IV iron improved 6MWD versus placebo (MD +26.0 m, 95% CI 18.1–33.9) and outperformed PO iron in symptom-related outcomes, while PO iron showed only a non-significant trend for 6MWD improvement (MD +35.1 m, 95% CI −5.2 to +75.4). <cite id="41080322">IV iron significantly improved 6MWD compared to placebo (MD +26.0 m; 95% CI: 18.1 to 33.9), whereas PO iron showed a comparable, but not statistically significant, mean improvement in 6MWD (MD +35.1 m; 95% CI: -5.2 to +75.4).</cite>

- Additional mechanistic signals support decongestion with IV iron. In FAIR-HF, IV FCM led to earlier reductions in weight and plasma volume status (PVS), suggesting fluid redistribution improvements that may enhance exercise tolerance and NYHA class over time. <cite id="31148411">At 4 weeks, FCM was associated with greater reductions in weight and PVS, and patients with decreased PVS from baseline to week 24 had larger 6MWD gains (61.4 m vs. 43.5 m) and higher rates of NYHA class improvement (33.3% vs. 15.5%).</cite>

# Evidence on Hospitalization and Mortality

- IV iron reduces HF hospitalizations. The CONFIRM-HF trial demonstrated a 61% relative risk reduction for worsening HF hospitalizations with IV FCM versus placebo (HR 0.39, 95% CI 0.19–0.82). <cite id="25176939">Treatment with FCM was associated with a significant reduction in the risk of hospitalizations for worsening HF (0.39, 95% CI 0.19–0.82, P = 0.009).</cite>

- Network meta-analysis indicates a modest but significant reduction in HF hospitalization risk with IV iron compared with placebo (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.66–0.93), with no clear mortality benefit overall. <cite id="41080322">IV iron reduced the risk of HF hospitalization (RR 0.79; 95% CI: 0.66 to 0.93). Neither IV nor PO iron was associated with a significant reduction in all-cause or cardiovascular mortality, although a trend toward benefit was observed with IV therapy.</cite>

- Budget-impact analyses align with clinical benefits. Pooled data from four RCTs showed FCM reduced hospitalizations for worsening HF (52 vs. 129 events over a year) and other resource use, yielding a minimal incremental annual budget per 1000 patients and supporting improved symptomatic status and shorter hospital stays. <cite id="28772041">The annual budget impact for FCM vs. no-iron therapy was €2,735,505 vs. €2,695,474 for 1000 patients, respectively, with fewer HF hospitalizations (52 vs. 129) and reduced outpatient and home visits; costs per 1000 patients decreased with FCM.</cite>

# Oral Iron vs. IV Iron

- PO iron shows inconsistent functional gains and weaker laboratory responses. Network meta-analysis found PO iron's 6MWD improvement was not statistically significant, and gains in ferritin and TSAT were inconsistent across trials. PO iron is frequently limited by gastrointestinal intolerance, whereas IV iron does not carry excess mortality or serious adverse events. <cite id="41080322">PO iron showed a non-significant mean improvement in 6MWD (MD +35.1 m; 95% CI: -5.2 to +75.4), with wider CIs and inconsistent ferritin and TSAT gains, and was primarily limited by gastrointestinal intolerance; adverse events were comparable across IV and PO, with no excess mortality or serious adverse events for IV iron.</cite>

- Efficacy is not preserved when restricting to specific subgroups. Trials in patients with and without anaemia show IV iron improves symptoms and functional capacity regardless of baseline haemoglobin, but safety and efficacy profiles are similar between groups, underscoring that benefits are not confined to anaemic subsets. <cite id="23787722">In FAIR-HF, FCM's effects on PGA and NYHA class at week 24 were similar in patients with and without anaemia, and safety (death or first hospitalization) was comparable between FCM and placebo in both anaemic and non-anaemic patients.</cite>

# Practical Implications

- Prefer IV iron for symptomatic HF with ID to maximize improvements in exercise capacity and reduce hospitalizations. IV iron's class effects include better 6MWD, NYHA class, ferritin, TSAT, and lower HF hospitalization risk, with acceptable safety. <cite id="41080322">IV iron significantly improved 6MWD, increased ferritin, improved TSAT, and reduced HF hospitalization risk compared with placebo, with moderate to high certainty and no excess mortality or serious adverse events.</cite> <cite id="25176939">In CONFIRM-HF, IV FCM improved 6MWD and NYHA class and reduced hospitalizations for worsening HF over 52 weeks without excess mortality or serious adverse events.</cite>

- Consider PO iron when IV therapy is not feasible, recognizing smaller and less consistent gains in exercise capacity and haemoglobin parameters, and higher rates of gastrointestinal intolerance. <cite id="41080322">PO iron ranked slightly higher for 6MWD in network analyses but showed inconsistent ferritin and TSAT gains and was limited by gastrointestinal intolerance, whereas IV iron ranked highest for hospitalization, ferritin, and TSAT outcomes.</cite>

# Bottom Line

For patients with heart failure and iron deficiency, IV iron therapy improves exercise capacity and reduces heart failure hospitalization rates more reliably than oral iron, which shows inconsistent functional benefits and weaker laboratory responses. IV iron should be the preferred approach when accessible and appropriate, with oral iron reserved for situations where IV therapy is not viable. <cite id="41080322">IV iron significantly improved 6MWD, increased ferritin, improved TSAT, and reduced HF hospitalization risk compared with placebo, while PO iron's benefits were inconsistent and often limited by gastrointestinal intolerance.</cite> <cite id="25176939">In a large randomized trial, IV FCM improved 6MWD and NYHA class and reduced hospitalizations for worsening HF without excess mortality or serious adverse events.</cite> <cite id="28772041">Budget and resource-use analyses are consistent with reduced and shorter hospitalizations and improved symptomatic status with IV FCM compared with no iron therapy.</cite>

data.title: Comparative Effectiveness and Safety of Intravenous Versus Oral Iron Therapy With Iron-Deficient Heart Failure: A Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
data.abstract: Iron deficiency (ID) is a common and clinically significant comorbidity in patients with heart failure (HF), contributing to reduced exercise capacity, poor quality of life, and increased hospitalization risk. Although intravenous (IV) iron therapy has demonstrated efficacy in improving functional outcomes, the comparative effectiveness of IV vs. oral (per os, or PO) iron supplementation remains uncertain. We conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA) of 13 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose, ferric derisomaltose, iron sucrose), PO iron (ferrous sulfate, ferrous fumarate, polysaccharide, sucrosomial, ferric polymaltose), and placebo in HF patients with ID, analyzed as route-specific class effects. Outcomes analyzed included six-minute walk distance (6MWD), ferritin, transferrin saturation (TSAT), HF hospitalization, all-cause mortality, and cardiovascular (CV) mortality. We used a Hartung-Knapp random-effects framework with Sidik-Jonkman variance, assessed heterogeneity and inconsistency using I 2 , τ 2 , design-by-treatment interaction, and node-splitting. Risk of bias was assessed independently by two reviewers using Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2), and certainty of evidence for all outcomes was graded using GRADE adapted for NMA. Because most contrasts included fewer than 10 RCTs, formal tests for publication bias were not feasible, and potential small-study effects were considered qualitatively in the GRADE assessments. Trials that reported outcomes only as medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs), or baseline values without follow-up data, were excluded from quantitative pooling and described narratively. IV iron significantly improved 6MWD compared to placebo (mean difference (MD) +26.0 m; 95% confidence interval (CI): 18.1 to 33.9), increased ferritin (MD +237.2 μg/L), and reduced the risk of HF hospitalization (risk ratio (RR) 0.79; 95% CI: 0.66 to 0.93), with moderate to high certainty. PO iron showed a comparable, but not statistically significant, mean improvement in 6MWD (MD +35.1 m; 95% CI: -5.2 to +75.4), with wider CIs and inconsistent ferritin and TSAT gains. Neither IV nor PO iron was associated with a significant reduction in all-cause or CV mortality, although a trend toward benefit was observed with IV therapy. Numerical SUCRA values favored IV iron for HF hospitalization (77.9 vs. 57.6 for PO, 14.5 for placebo), ferritin (100.0 vs. 50.0 vs. 0.0), and TSAT (74.0 vs. 75.8 vs. 0.2), while PO iron ranked slightly higher for 6MWD (76.3 vs. 73.7 vs. 0.0). Included PO formulations encompassed both traditional preparations (ferrous sulfate/fumarate, polysaccharide) and newer agents such as sucrosomial iron and ferric polymaltose. Adverse events were comparable across groups: IV iron was not associated with excess mortality or serious adverse events, and PO iron was primarily limited by gastrointestinal intolerance. Sensitivity analyses restricting outcomes to trials with 3-12 months of follow-up showed consistent results, while longer studies mainly influenced event counts rather than the direction of effect. Our findings support the use of IV iron as the preferred strategy to improve symptoms and reduce hospitalizations in HF patients with ID, whereas PO iron may be considered when IV therapy is inaccessible. Further large-scale trials are needed to clarify long-term mortality impact and the role of newer PO formulations.

data.title: Budget impact of intravenous iron therapy with ferric carboxymaltose in patients with chronic heart failure and iron deficiency in Germany.
data.abstract:
AIMS
Treatment of iron deficiency (ID) in patients with heart failure (HF) with intravenous iron substitution [ferric carboxymaltose (FCM)] has previously shown significant improvements in exercise capacity, New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class, quality of life, and reduction of hospitalization. The aim of this study was to estimate the budget impact of FCM treatment for patients with HF and ID.
METHODS AND RESULTS
Individual patient data from four double-blind randomized controlled trials were pooled for this analysis. Expected outcomes were modelled for a treatment period of 1 year, using multivariate statistical methods. Associated unit costs were derived from claims data. Budget impact was calculated from the perspective of the Statutory Health Insurance. Multiple deterministic sensitivity analyses were performed. The annual budget impact for therapy with FCM vs. no-iron therapy was €2 735 505 and €2 695 474 for 1000 patients, respectively, resulting in additional annual costs of €40.03 for each treated patient. Main costs drivers are the FCM treatment cost and cost of hospitalizations due to HF worsening. FCM therapy compared with no-iron therapy resulted in reduced cost per 1000 patients: for reduced hospitalization due to HF worsening (52 vs. 129 hospitalizations amounting to €230 591 vs. €597 078), for reduced other medication (€1 611 007 vs. €1 679 908), fewer outpatient visits (€332 523 vs. €378 019), and home visits (€29 627 vs. €40 469). Sensitivity analyses showed robustness of the results.
CONCLUSIONS
Therapy with FCM has a minimal budget impact of €40 031 per 1000 patients per year. This budget impact translates into reduced and shorter hospitalizations and improved symptomatic status of the patients.

In a large randomized trial (CONFIRM-HF), IV ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) increased 6MWD by 33 m at 24 weeks versus placebo, with effects sustained at 52 weeks (+36 m). Improvements in NYHA class, patient global assessment, quality of life, and fatigue were observed from 24 weeks onward. IV FCM also reduced hospitalizations for worsening HF (hazard ratio 0.39, 95% CI 0.19–0.82) without increasing mortality or serious adverse events. <cite id="25176939">Treatment with FCM significantly prolonged 6MWD at Week 24 (difference FCM vs. placebo: 33 ± 11 m, P = 0.002), with effects sustained to Week 52 (36 ± 11 m, P < 0.001), and was associated with a significant reduction in hospitalizations for worsening HF (0.39, 95% CI 0.19–0.82, P = 0.009), while deaths and adverse events were comparable.</cite>

- Network meta-analysis corroborates IV iron's functional benefits. IV iron improved 6MWD versus placebo (MD +26.0 m, 95% CI 18.1–33.9) and outperformed PO iron in symptom-related outcomes, while PO iron showed only a non-significant trend for 6MWD improvement (MD +35.1 m, 95% CI −5.2 to +75.4). <cite id="41080322">IV iron significantly improved 6MWD compared to placebo (MD +26.0 m; 95% CI: 18.1 to 33.9), whereas PO iron showed a comparable, but not statistically significant, mean improvement in 6MWD (MD +35.1 m; 95% CI: -5.2 to +75.4).</cite>

- Additional mechanistic signals support decongestion with IV iron. In FAIR-HF, IV FCM led to earlier reductions in weight and plasma volume status (PVS), suggesting fluid redistribution improvements that may enhance exercise tolerance and NYHA class over time. <cite id="31148411">At 4 weeks, FCM was associated with greater reductions in weight and PVS, and patients with decreased PVS from baseline to week 24 had larger 6MWD gains (61.4 m vs. 43.5 m) and higher rates of NYHA class improvement (33.3% vs. 15.5%).</cite>

# Evidence on Hospitalization and Mortality

- IV iron reduces HF hospitalizations. The CONFIRM-HF trial demonstrated a 61% relative risk reduction for worsening HF hospitalizations with IV FCM versus placebo (HR 0.39, 95% CI 0.19–0.82). <cite id="25176939">Treatment with FCM was associated with a significant reduction in the risk of hospitalizations for worsening HF (0.39, 95% CI 0.19–0.82, P = 0.009).</cite>

- Network meta-analysis indicates a modest but significant reduction in HF hospitalization risk with IV iron compared with placebo (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.66–0.93), with no clear mortality benefit overall. <cite id="41080322">IV iron reduced the risk of HF hospitalization (RR 0.79; 95% CI: 0.66 to 0.93). Neither IV nor PO iron was associated with a significant reduction in all-cause or cardiovascular mortality, although a trend toward benefit was observed with IV therapy.</cite>

- Budget-impact analyses align with clinical benefits. Pooled data from four RCTs showed FCM reduced hospitalizations for worsening HF (52 vs. 129 events over a year) and other resource use, yielding a minimal incremental annual budget per 1000 patients and supporting improved symptomatic status and shorter hospital stays. <cite id="28772041">The annual budget impact for FCM vs. no-iron therapy was €2,735,505 vs. €2,695,474 for 1000 patients, respectively, with fewer HF hospitalizations (52 vs. 129) and reduced outpatient and home visits; costs per 1000 patients decreased with FCM.</cite>

# Oral Iron vs. IV Iron

- PO iron shows inconsistent functional gains and weaker laboratory responses. Network meta-analysis found PO iron's 6MWD improvement was not statistically significant, and gains in ferritin and TSAT were inconsistent across trials. PO iron is frequently limited by gastrointestinal intolerance, whereas IV iron does not carry excess mortality or serious adverse events. <cite id="41080322">PO iron showed a non-significant mean improvement in 6MWD (MD +35.1 m; 95% CI: -5.2 to +75.4), with wider CIs and inconsistent ferritin and TSAT gains, and was primarily limited by gastrointestinal intolerance; adverse events were comparable across IV and PO, with no excess mortality or serious adverse events for IV iron.</cite>

- Efficacy is not preserved when restricting to specific subgroups. Trials in patients with and without anaemia show IV iron improves symptoms and functional capacity regardless of baseline haemoglobin, but safety and efficacy profiles are similar between groups, underscoring that benefits are not confined to anaemic subsets. <cite id="23787722">In FAIR-HF, FCM's effects on PGA and NYHA class at week 24 were similar in patients with and without anaemia, and safety (death or first hospitalization) was comparable between FCM and placebo in both anaemic and non-anaemic patients.</cite>

# Practical Implications

- Prefer IV iron for symptomatic HF with ID to maximize improvements in exercise capacity and reduce hospitalizations. IV iron's class effects include better 6MWD, NYHA class, ferritin, TSAT, and lower HF hospitalization risk, with acceptable safety. <cite id="41080322">IV iron significantly improved 6MWD, increased ferritin, improved TSAT, and reduced HF hospitalization risk compared with placebo, with moderate to high certainty and no excess mortality or serious adverse events.</cite> <cite id="25176939">In CONFIRM-HF, IV FCM improved 6MWD and NYHA class and reduced hospitalizations for worsening HF over 52 weeks without excess mortality or serious adverse events.</cite>

- Consider PO iron when IV therapy is not feasible, recognizing smaller and less consistent gains in exercise capacity and haemoglobin parameters, and higher rates of gastrointestinal intolerance. <cite id="41080322">PO iron ranked slightly higher for 6MWD in network analyses but showed inconsistent ferritin and TSAT gains and was limited by gastrointestinal intolerance, whereas IV iron ranked highest for hospitalization, ferritin, and TSAT outcomes.</cite>

# Bottom Line

For patients with heart failure and iron deficiency, IV iron therapy improves exercise capacity and reduces heart failure hospitalization rates more reliably than oral iron, which shows inconsistent functional benefits and weaker laboratory responses. IV iron should be the preferred approach when accessible and appropriate, with oral iron reserved for situations where IV therapy is not viable. <cite id="41080322">IV iron significantly improved 6MWD, increased ferritin, improved TSAT, and reduced HF hospitalization risk compared with placebo, while PO iron's benefits were inconsistent and often limited by gastrointestinal intolerance.</cite> <cite id="25176939">In a large randomized trial, IV FCM improved 6MWD and NYHA class and reduced hospitalizations for worsening HF without excess mortality or serious adverse events.</cite> <cite id="28772041">Budget and resource-use analyses are consistent with reduced and shorter hospitalizations and improved symptomatic status with IV FCM compared with no iron therapy.</cite>
